title: Yes, Europe Is a Middle Power, Too
gist: Chatham House's Galip Dalay uses the Iran war to argue that Europe has become a middle power and must adopt a new 'state psychology' of cross-regional cooperation, since Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar and Oman — not the E3 — drove the war's diplomacy. He predicts Iran's weaponization of the Strait of Hormuz will backfire as the Hejaz Railway and a revived Iraq-Syria crude pipeline structurally reroute trade away from the chokepoint.

insights.claim: By weaponizing its geography through the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran acquired immense short-term strategic leverage, but the strategy is likely to backfire over the medium to long term as regional states reroute their geographies and the strait's strategic value declines relatively.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: The Hormuz risk premium is a decaying asset over a multi-year horizon: near-term spikes are real but rerouting capex permanently reduces the chokepoint's pricing power.
insights.quote: Iran may have won the psychological war, but it could still lose the strategic one.

insights.claim: The Hormuz crisis gave additional impetus and urgency to the Hejaz Railway project, which will connect the Gulf to Turkey and Europe via a land route.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: A Gulf-to-Europe land corridor is a multi-decade infrastructure buildout with contractor, rail and logistics beneficiaries in Turkey and the Gulf — track project financing announcements.

insights.claim: Under U.S. supervision, Iraq and Syria signed a deal to revive a crude oil pipeline project that will let Iraqi oil reach the Mediterranean via Syria, partially reducing the impact of the Hormuz closure.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: An operational Iraq-Syria-Mediterranean line adds non-Hormuz export capacity and is bearish for the structural Gulf freight and war-risk premium once flowing.

insights.claim: Although a country's geography is static, its meaning can change dynamically because states and regions can reimagine and redesign their geographies to reduce dependencies.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Chokepoint leverage is endogenous: using it accelerates its own obsolescence, a reusable model for any infrastructure or supply-chain monopoly.

themes.theme: The autonomy-alliance trap for Gulf states

insights.claim: The alliance with the United States made Gulf middle powers such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates targets of Iranian attacks and cost them breaches of their security and sovereignty, while simultaneously deepening their short-term dependence on Washington.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Gulf states are locked into a partner that both attracts attacks and is required to defend against them — a dependency that drives near-term U.S. defense purchases even amid resentment.
insights.locator: The United States’ war against Iran has also laid bare

insights.claim: Middle powers have concluded that the United States, though still indispensable, is too unreliable and unpredictable to be fully depended on for security partnerships and defense industry cooperation.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Structural diversification of defense procurement away from U.S. primes is now consensus among middle powers — a durable multi-year revenue shift to non-U.S. defense suppliers.
insights.locator: Consequently, middle powers have learned

insights.claim: Gulf states will probably seek deeper security ties and defense industry cooperation with partners that will not trigger U.S. wrath, specifically Pakistan, Turkey, European powers such as France, the United Kingdom and Italy, plus Ukraine and South Korea.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: A named beneficiary list for Gulf defense contracts — Turkish, Korean, Italian, French and UK defense firms and Ukraine's drone sector are the order-flow candidates.
insights.locator: The Gulf states will probably seek deeper security ties

insights.claim: The new era requires pooling agency and autonomy at the Gulf Cooperation Council level rather than at the individual country level, using the European Union and ASEAN as models of regional-level agency.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Deeper GCC integration on defense and procurement would consolidate buying power and change how Gulf defense and infrastructure contracts are awarded.
insights.locator: The new era requires better security coordination

insights.claim: GCC states cannot afford to adopt the same policy approach to Iran as the United States and Israel because their locations leave them permanently vulnerable, and the same dilemma governs Southeast Asian approaches to China and Central Asian approaches to Russia.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Proximate states will always hedge rather than fully align, so U.S. or allied coalition-building assumptions that discount geography will keep disappointing.
insights.quote: Geographic proximity magnifies the cost of adversarial relations for middle powers.

insights.claim: Iran implicitly and explicitly regards the Gulf as its sphere of influence and seeks to rewrite the region's rules, which will only produce greater regional fragmentation, counterbalancing strategies and more external intervention.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Iranian sphere-of-influence assertion is self-defeating in that it invites the very external military presence it seeks to expel — expect a more, not less, militarized Gulf.
insights.locator: The dangers of spheres-of-influence logic

insights.claim: Sphere-of-influence geopolitics involves not only geopolitical reconfiguration of a region but its normative reconfiguration in the image of the sphere's hegemon, which further erodes the agency of small and middle powers.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Spheres of influence carry regulatory and normative capture, not just security costs — relevant to how standards and rules get set in contested regions.

insights.claim: The countries that sought active diplomatic resolution to the Iran war were non-Western — Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar and Oman — while European middle powers were absent from Iran, Gaza and Ukraine diplomacy alike.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Deal catalysts now come from Doha, Muscat, Ankara and Islamabad; monitoring those capitals gives earlier signal on cease-fires than watching Brussels or Geneva.
insights.locator: The countries that sought active diplomatic resolution

insights.claim: European absence from Iran diplomacy is glaring given that the E3 — the United Kingdom, France and Germany — initiated the nuclear diplomacy in 2003 that led to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, one of the signature achievements of European diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Europe's loss of its one proven Middle East diplomatic franchise is a concrete measure of declining EU geopolitical relevance and of who holds sanctions-relief leverage now.
insights.locator: Given that the E3

insights.claim: Geneva, once the center of international diplomacy, now barely features in contemporary diplomacy and mediation efforts to settle wars or conflicts, reflecting a broader retreat of Western actors and multilateral organizations from mediation and peacemaking.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: The institutional venue for conflict resolution has shifted to Gulf and Turkish capitals, with knock-on implications for where legal, financial and advisory services around settlements are transacted.
insights.quote: Geneva, once the center of international diplomacy, now barely features in contemporary diplomacy and mediation efforts to settle wars or conflicts.

insights.claim: For small or middle powers, international law and norms are not luxury goods but functional necessities, which is why they carry the diplomatic and peacemaking burden that great powers abandon.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Middle powers are the structural constituency for rules-based institutions, so their coalitions are where any residual multilateral enforcement will come from.
insights.quote: For small or middle powers, international law and norms are not luxury goods.

themes.theme: State psychology and the north-south asymmetry

insights.claim: Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defense for policy, dismissed the very idea of a middle powers strategy as a costly distraction in social media posts, with the disparagement directed largely at Canada and Europe rather than at non-Western middle powers.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Senior Pentagon policy hostility to middle-power coalitions signals Washington will not underwrite them, forcing allied hedging to proceed without U.S. blessing.
insights.locator: Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby’s recent

insights.claim: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's Davos speech calling on middle powers to band together brought the middle-power concept to the forefront of global policy debate this year.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Middle-power coalition-building has explicit top-level political sponsorship, making it a live institutional agenda rather than an academic one.
insights.locator: It’s been an unusual year for middle powers

insights.claim: For post-colonial global south states, becoming a middle power signals increased agency and higher status, whereas for post-imperial UN Security Council veto-holders such as the United Kingdom and France it registers as a decline in status — an asymmetry that blocks joint action.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: The psychological asymmetry explains why north-south middle-power coalitions keep failing to form, and why UK and French adjustment will be slow and reluctant.
insights.locator: For countries in the global south

insights.claim: European middle powers typically invite global south actors to join frameworks Europe has already developed, an approach that reads as hierarchy rather than equality and is increasingly anathema in the global south.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: EU regulatory export strategy — the Brussels effect — is hitting political resistance, which weakens Europe's ability to set global standards in AI, climate and trade.
insights.locator: Most of the time, European middle powers invite

insights.claim: Middle powers in the global north are largely fearful of the emerging world while those in the global south are more hopeful, because global south states view great-power rivalry and multipolarity as expanding their room for hedging and balancing.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Emerging-market governments will keep monetizing multipolarity through competitive bidding between blocs rather than picking a side — a persistent feature, not a phase.
insights.locator: Similar asymmetry is evident in middle powers’

insights.claim: The world is moving toward multi-ordering rather than merely multipolarity, so shared global norms, standards and regulations can only be achieved through mutual creation rather than by exporting European standards.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Multi-ordering implies competing regulatory regimes rather than one contested pole — companies should plan for parallel compliance stacks, not convergence.
insights.locator: In a world moving toward multi-ordering

insights.claim: Middle powers cannot prevent the unilateralism and militarism of great powers as shown by the Iran, Ukraine and Gaza wars, but they can change the global order's security-centric agenda, priorities and language if they work together.
insights.speaker: Galip Dalay
insights.so_what: Expect middle-power influence to show up in agenda-setting on food security, arms control, climate and AI rather than in conflict prevention — calibrate expectations to that channel.
insights.quote: The middle powers must chart a course that is both humble and ambitious.
insights.locator: Middle powers may have learned they can’t reshuffle
